claim: Citrate, α-ketoglutarate and succinate are TCA cycle intermediates.
source: Citrate, α-ketoglutarate and succinate are TCA cycle intermediates that also play essential roles in metabolic signaling and cellular regulation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: Citrate, α-ketoglutarate and succinate play essential roles in metabolic signaling and cellular regulation.
source: Citrate, α-ketoglutarate and succinate are TCA cycle intermediates that also play essential roles in metabolic signaling and cellular regulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the Introduction section.

claim: Di- and tricarboxylates are imported into the cell by the DASS family of plasma membrane transporters.
source: These di- and tricarboxylates are imported into the cell by the divalent anion sodium symporter (DASS) family of plasma membrane transporters, which contains both cotransporters and exchangers.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The DASS family contains both cotransporters and exchangers.
source: These di- and tricarboxylates are imported into the cell by the divalent anion sodium symporter (DASS) family of plasma membrane transporters, which contains both cotransporters and exchangers.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and citations.

claim: DASS proteins transport substrates via an elevator mechanism.
source: While DASS proteins transport substrates via an elevator mechanism, to date structures are only available for a single DASS cotransporter protein in a substrate-bound, inward-facing state.
evidence: This is supported by structural information and cross-linking data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Prior to this work, structures were only available for a single DASS cotransporter protein in a substrate-bound, inward-facing state.
source: While DASS proteins transport substrates via an elevator mechanism, to date structures are only available for a single DASS cotransporter protein in a substrate-bound, inward-facing state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous VcINDY structures.

claim: The authors report multiple cryo-EM and X-ray structures in four different states, including three hitherto unseen states.
source: We report multiple cryo-EM and X-ray structures in four different states, including three hitherto unseen states, along with molecular dynamics simulations, of both a cotransporter and an exchanger.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript (Tables 1 and 2, Figures 1 and 2).

claim: Comparison of outward- and inward-facing structures reveals how the transport domain translates and rotates within the framework of the scaffold domain through the transport cycle.
source: Comparison of these outward- and inward-facing structures reveal how the transport domain translates and rotates within the framework of the scaffold domain through the transport cycle.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons and MD simulations presented in the manuscript (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: DASS transporters ensure substrate coupling by a charge-compensation mechanism.
source: Additionally, we propose that DASS transporters ensure substrate coupling by a charge-compensation mechanism, and by structural changes upon substrate release.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations and inference from the data.

claim: DASS transporters ensure substrate coupling by structural changes upon substrate release.
source: Additionally, we propose that DASS transporters ensure substrate coupling by a charge-compensation mechanism, and by structural changes upon substrate release.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons between substrate-bound and substrate-free states (Figure 7).

claim: Citrate acts as a precursor of fatty acid synthesis.
source: In particular, citrate acts as a precursor of fatty acid synthesis and allosterically regulates both fatty acid synthesis and glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Citrate allosterically regulates both fatty acid synthesis and glycolysis.
source: In particular, citrate acts as a precursor of fatty acid synthesis and allosterically regulates both fatty acid synthesis and glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Citrate is used to synthesize acetyl-CoA for histone acetylation.
source: Citrate is also used to synthesize acetyl-CoA for histone acetylation and is therefore essential for the regulation of DNA transcription and replication (Wellen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009.

claim: Citrate is essential for the regulation of DNA transcription and replication.
source: Citrate is also used to synthesize acetyl-CoA for histone acetylation and is therefore essential for the regulation of DNA transcription and replication (Wellen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009.

claim: Naive embryonic stem cells that exhibit an elevated αKG-to-succinate ratio maintain pluripotency.
source: Naive embryonic stem cells that exhibit an elevated αKG-to-succinate ratio maintain pluripotency (Carey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carey et al., 2015.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells with p53-deficiency have a lowered αKG-to-succinate ratio.
source: In contrast, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells with p53-deficiency have a lowed αKG-to-succinate ratio, and increasing the cellular concentration of αKG leads to a phenotype similar to that of tumor suppression by p53 restoration (Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morris et al., 2019.

claim: Increasing the cellular concentration of αKG in p53-deficient pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells leads to a phenotype similar to that of tumor suppression by p53 restoration.
source: In contrast, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells with p53-deficiency have a lowed αKG-to-succinate ratio, and increasing the cellular concentration of αKG leads to a phenotype similar to that of tumor suppression by p53 restoration (Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morris et al., 2019.

claim: Mammalian cells import di- and tricarboxylates from the bloodstream via NaCT, NaDC1, and NaDC3.
source: Mammalian cells import di- and tricarboxylates from the bloodstream via the Na+-dependent citrate transporter (NaCT) and the Na+-dependent dicarboxylate transporters 1 and 3 (NaDC1 and NaDC3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markovich and Murer, 2004; Bergeron et al., 2013; Pajor, 2014.

claim: NaCT, NaDC1, and NaDC3 belong to the solute carrier 13 (SLC13) gene family.
source: These plasma membrane proteins belong to the solute carrier 13 (SLC13) gene family (Markovich and Murer, 2004; Bergeron et al., 2013; Pajor, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markovich and Murer, 2004; Bergeron et al., 2013; Pajor, 2014.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in the human NaCT transporter cause a type of encephalopathy (SLC13A5 Deficiency).
source: Loss-of-function mutations in the human NaCT transporter cause a type of encephalopathy (SLC13A5 Deficiency) (Thevenon et al., 2014; Hardies et al., 2015; Klotz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thevenon et al., 2014; Hardies et al., 2015; Klotz et al., 2016.

claim: Knocking out NaCT in mice leads to protection from obesity and insulin resistance.
source: In contrast, knocking out NaCT in mice leads to protection from obesity and insulin resistance, while mutations in the homologous fly gene extends their lifespan (Birkenfeld et al., 2011; Rogina et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birkenfeld et al., 2011; Rogina et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in the homologous fly gene to NaCT extend fly lifespan.
source: In contrast, knocking out NaCT in mice leads to protection from obesity and insulin resistance, while mutations in the homologous fly gene extends their lifespan (Birkenfeld et al., 2011; Rogina et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rogina et al., 2000.

claim: Variants in the dicarboxylate transporter NaDC3 cause acute reversible leukoencephalopathy, with accumulation of αKG in the cerebrospinal fluid and urine.
source: Variants in the dicarboxylate transporter NaDC3 cause acute reversible leukoencephalopathy, with accumulation of αKG in the cerebrospinal fluid and urine (Dewulf et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dewulf et al., 2019.

claim: The central roles of SLC13 proteins in cell metabolism and signaling make them attractive targets for treating obesity, diabetes, cancer and epilepsy.
source: These central roles of SLC13 proteins in cell metabolism and signaling make them particularly attractive targets for treating obesity, diabetes, cancer and epilepsy (Huard et al., 2015; Pajor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huard et al., 2015; Pajor et al., 2016.

claim: Mammalian SLC13 proteins are members of the larger divalent-anion sodium symporter (DASS) family.
source: The mammalian SLC13 proteins are members of the larger divalent-anion sodium symporter (DASS) family (Markovich and Murer, 2004; Bergeron et al., 2013; Pajor, 2014; Prakash et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markovich and Murer, 2004; Bergeron et al., 2013; Pajor, 2014; Prakash et al., 2003.

claim: DASS proteins typically have a molecular weight of 45–65 kDa.
source: DASS proteins typically have a molecular weight of 45–65 kDa and form obligate homodimers.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: DASS proteins form obligate homodimers.
source: DASS proteins typically have a molecular weight of 45–65 kDa and form obligate homodimers.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).

claim: The majority of DASS proteins are Na+-coupled cotransporters with a transport stoichiometry of one substrate to 2–4 Na+ ions.
source: The majority of DASS proteins are Na+-coupled cotransporters with a transport stoichiometry of one substrate to 2–4 Na+ ions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Some DASS members are exchangers that typically exchange succinate for other dicarboxylates.
source: However, other DASS members are exchangers (Pos et al., 1998), typically exchanging succinate for other dicarboxylates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pos et al., 1998 and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: DASS cotransporters and exchangers separate into distinct clades on a phylogenetic tree and are named DASS-C and DASS-E.
source: While sequence analysis strongly suggests a shared fold (Lolkema and Slotboom, 1998), these two groups separate into distinct clades on a phylogenetic tree and are thereby named DASS-C and DASS-E for cotransporter/symporter and exchanger/antiporter, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and a citation to Lolkema and Slotboom, 1998.

claim: All available DASS structures prior to this work are of VcINDY in an inward-facing (Ci-Na+-S) state.
source: All available DASS structures are of the Na+-driven dicarboxylate transporter VcINDY from Vibrio cholerae, in an inward-facing (Ci-Na+-S) state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f; Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f.

claim: Each VcINDY protomer consists of a scaffold and a transport domain.
source: Each protomer consists of a scaffold and a transport domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: In the VcINDY transport domain, the two carboxylate moieties of the bound substrate are coordinated by two conserved Ser-Asn-Thr (SNT) motifs.
source: In the transport domain, the two carboxylate moieties of the bound substrate are coordinated by two conserved Ser-Asn-Thr (SNT) motifs, which also form part of the Na+-binding sites Na1 and Na2.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The SNT motifs in VcINDY also form part of the Na+-binding sites Na1 and Na2.
source: In the transport domain, the two carboxylate moieties of the bound substrate are coordinated by two conserved Ser-Asn-Thr (SNT) motifs, which also form part of the Na+-binding sites Na1 and Na2.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Structural information, cross-linking and computer modeling indicate that DASS proteins operate in an elevator-type transport mechanism.
source: Structural information, along with cross-linking and computer modeling (Mancusso et al., 2012; Mulligan et al., 2016), indicates that DASS proteins operate in an elevator-type transport mechanism (Figure 1a; Reyes et al., 2009; Drew and Boudker, 2016; Garaeva and Slotboom, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mancusso et al., 2012; Mulligan et al., 2016; Reyes et al., 2009; Drew and Boudker, 2016; Garaeva and Slotboom, 2020 and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Without the structure of an outward-facing conformation, a detailed description of the changes between the Co and Ci conformations for DASS proteins remains lacking.
source: However, without the structure of an outward-facing (Co) conformation structure, a detailed description of the changes between the Co and Ci conformations for DASS proteins remains lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this work.

claim: How DASS exchangers translocate substrates across the membrane is completely unknown.
source: How DASS exchangers translocate the substrates across the membrane is completely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this work.

claim: Studies on DASS-C cotransporters show that these proteins sequentially bind sodium and then substrate, with this order being reversed during the release process.
source: Studies on multiple DASS-C cotransporters using transport kinetics, electrophysiology and chemical cross-linking have shown that these proteins sequentially bind sodium and then substrate, with this order being reversed during the release process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Wright et al., 1983; Yao and Pajor, 2000; Hall and Pajor, 2005; Pajor et al., 2013; Mulligan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wright et al., 1983; Yao and Pajor, 2000; Hall and Pajor, 2005; Pajor et al., 2013; Mulligan et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The arrangement of the substrate and Na+-sites in the VcINDY Ci-Na+-S state is consistent with a sequential binding mechanism.
source: The arrangement of the observed substrate and Na+-sites in the known VcINDY Ci-Na+-S state is also consistent with such a mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: It is unclear how Na+ slippage is avoided in DASS cotransporters.
source: However, it is unclear how Na+ slippage is avoided, namely, how the transporter undergoes interconversion between the apo Ci and Co states only, and between the fully loaded Ci-Na+-S and Co-Na+-S states, but not between the Na+-only loaded Ci-Na+ and Co-Na+ states.
evidence: This is a statement about an unresolved question in the field.

claim: Understanding the mechanism of Na+ slippage avoidance is essential to understanding the mechanism of SLC13 family disease mutations and the design of drugs to manipulate di- and tricarboxylate import.
source: This information is essential to understanding the mechanism of SLC13 family disease mutations and the design of drugs to manipulate di- and tricarboxylate import.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the research question.

claim: The authors hypothesize that DASS-E exchangers follow a typical antiport kinetic mechanism.
source: For the DASS-E exchangers, which we hypothesize follow a typical antiport kinetic mechanism (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), it is even less clear how they translocate the substrates across the membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The authors aimed to characterize the structural basis of the entire transport cycle of the DASS family using cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography, MD simulations and transport activity assays.
source: We aimed to characterize the structural basis of the entire transport cycle of the DASS family using a combination of single particle cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and transport activity assays.
evidence: This is a statement of the research objectives.

claim: VcINDY has exclusively been observed in a Ci-Na+-S state prior to this work.
source: The only structurally characterized DASS transporter, VcINDY, has exclusively been observed in a Ci-Na+-S state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e; Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The authors purified VcINDY in 100 mM Na+ without substrate for cryo-EM to obtain a substrate-free, Na+-bound state structure.
source: To obtain the structure of a DASS protein in a substrate-free, Na+-bound state, we purified VcINDY in 100 mM Na+, but in the absence of a substrate, for single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The total mass of a VcINDY dimer is only 96 kDa, with almost all of it embedded in the membrane.
source: The total mass of a VcINDY dimer is only 96 kDa, and almost that entire mass is embedded in the membrane.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the protein sequence and structure.

claim: The small size of VcINDY posed a challenge for single-particle analysis.
source: This posed a challenge for single-particle analysis, and therefore we used two separate strategies for cryo-EM sample preparation.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges of the study.

claim: The authors used Fab84 to increase the effective particle mass of VcINDY for cryo-EM.
source: The first was to increase the effective particle mass using a synthetic antibody fragment (Fab). Using VcINDY reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs, we screened for Fabs using phage display technology (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a; Fellouse et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2012). In this way we identified Fab84, which was subsequently overexpressed, purified, and mixed with VcINDY in nanodiscs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2a-c and citations.

claim: The VcINDY-Fab84 structure was determined to 3.15 Å resolution.
source: The VcINDY-Fab84 structure was determined to 3.15 Å resolution (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d,e and h, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d,e,h and Table 1.

claim: The authors used amphipol polymer to preserve VcINDY for cryo-EM.
source: In a parallel approach, we used amphipol polymer (Huynh et al., 2018) to preserve the transporter protein (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2f,g & k, and Table 1), which allowed data collection on particularly thin ice to maximize signal-to-noise.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, supported by Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2f,g,k and Table 1, and a citation to Huynh et al., 2018.

claim: The VcINDY structure in amphipol was determined to 3.16 Å resolution.
source: This VcINDY structure in amphipol, without Fab, was determined to 3.16 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2f,g,k and Table 1.

claim: Both VcINDY cryo-EM maps are at sufficiently high resolution and quality to allow direct model building.
source: Both maps are at a sufficiently high resolution and quality to allow direct model building, and the structures are nearly identical (r.m.s.d. 0.750 Å).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and model quality statistics in Table 1.

claim: The VcINDY-Fab84 and VcINDY-amphipol structures are nearly identical with an r.m.s.d. of 0.750 Å.
source: Both maps are at a sufficiently high resolution and quality to allow direct model building, and the structures are nearly identical (r.m.s.d. 0.750 Å).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two structures.

claim: The authors crystallized VcINDY in complex with sodium and terephthalate and solved the X-ray structure to 3.92 Å resolution.
source: Finally, to obtain clear density of substrate in the binding site of VcINDY, we crystallized the protein in complex with sodium and terephthalate, and solved the X-ray structure to 3.92 Å resolution by molecular replacement (Figure 1d and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 1d and Table 2.

claim: The authors hypothesized that terephthalate would bind within the VcINDY binding site and provide stronger electron density than native substrates.
source: With two carboxylate moieties at approximately the same distance as those of native substrates, we hypothesized the terephthalate would bind within the VcINDY binding site, while its large benzene ring would provide stronger electron density than succinate, fumarate, or malate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on the chemical structure of terephthalate.

claim: LaINDY was able to support aerobic growth on αKG as the sole carbon source for an E. coli strain in which the only aerobically expressed αKG transporter was knocked out.
source: LaINDY was able to support aerobic growth on αKG as the sole carbon source for an E. coli strain in which the only aerobically expressed αKG transporter was knocked out (Baba et al., 2006; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and a citation to Baba et al., 2006.

claim: E. coli transformed with LaINDY accumulated radioactive succinate from an external solution.
source: E. coli transformed with LaINDY accumulated radioactive succinate from an external solution, likely in exchange for endogenous internal dicarboxylates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the transport assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Addition of excess external succinate or αKG reduced the amount of internalized radioactive succinate due to LaINDY-facilitated dicarboxylate exchange.
source: Subsequent addition of excess external succinate or αKG reduced the amount of internalized radioactive succinate due to LaINDY-facilitated dicarboxylate exchange (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the transport assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The authors screened various VcINDY homologs and chose LaINDY to obtain the structure of a DASS protein in its Co conformation.
source: To obtain the structure of a DASS protein in its Co conformation, we screened various VcINDY homologs and chose a DASS-E protein from Lactobacillus acidophilus (LaINDY) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The LaINDY map obtained in amphipol was at 3.09 Å resolution, allowing for direct model building.
source: The LaINDY map obtained in this way was at 3.09 Å resolution, allowing for direct model building (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–i, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–i and Table 1.

claim: The LaINDY structure was in an outward-facing Co state.
source: Notably, the LaINDY structure was in an outward-facing Co state.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The authors examined the thermostability and monodispersity of LaINDY at elevated temperatures in the presence of various potential substrates and substrate analogs to identify substrates suitable for structure determination.
source: Next, we attempted to determine the structure of LaINDY in its substrate-bound state. To identify substrates suitable for structure determination of such a complex, we examined the thermostability and monodispersity of LaINDY at elevated temperatures in the presence of various potential substrates and substrate analogs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Malate and αKG were identified as stabilizers of LaINDY.
source: Following identification of malate and αKG as stabilizers, we determined cryo-EM maps of LaINDY in complex with each to 3.36 Å and 3.71 Å, respectively (Figure 2c & d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j & k, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the thermostability assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The authors determined cryo-EM maps of LaINDY in complex with malate to 3.36 Å and with αKG to 3.71 Å.
source: Following identification of malate and αKG as stabilizers, we determined cryo-EM maps of LaINDY in complex with each to 3.36 Å and 3.71 Å, respectively (Figure 2c & d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j & k, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2c & d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j & k and Table 1.

claim: The authors solved a 2.85 Å X-ray structure of LaINDY in the presence of both malate and αKG.
source: We also solved a 2.85 Å X-ray structure of LaINDY in the presence of both malate and αKG (Figure 2e and Table 2), using the LaINDY-αKG cryo-EM structure as the search model for molecular replacement.
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 2e and Table 2.

claim: All three LaINDY complex structures were in an outward-facing Co-S state.
source: As with the apo LaINDY structure, all three LaINDY complex structures were in an outward-facing Co-S state.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 2c-e.

claim: The authors used a custom biased MD simulation protocol to drive LaINDY to a Ci-S target model suggested by LaINDY's internal inverted repeat topological symmetry.
source: Finally, to characterize the Co-S to Ci-S transition of a DASS protein, we used a custom biased MD simulation protocol (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary Note) to drive LaINDY to a Ci-S target model suggested by LaINDY's internal inverted repeat topological symmetry (Video 1 and Supplementary Note).
evidence: This is a description of the computational approach, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and Video 1.

claim: The authors bookended the induced transition with unbiased MD simulations of LaINDY's Co-S and Ci-S states.
source: We bookended this induced transition with unbiased MD simulations of LaINDY's Co-S and Ci-S states (Video 2), which enabled us to characterize LaINDY's equilibrium structural dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of the computational approach, supported by Video 2.

claim: The 3.09 Å cryo-EM map of LaINDY determined in the absence of substrate shows the transporter in its Co apo state.
source: The 3.09 Å cryo-EM map of LaINDY determined in the absence of substrate shows the transporter in its Co apo state (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The LaINDY cryo-EM map shows a transporter dimer, in agreement with LaINDY's apparent mass in detergent solution.
source: In agreement with LaINDY's apparent mass in detergent solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), the map shows a transporter dimer.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3a and b and the mass measurement shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Each LaINDY protomer consists of a scaffold domain and a transport domain.
source: Each protomer consists of a scaffold domain and a transport domain.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The transmembrane topology and domain organization of LaINDY resemble that of VcINDY.
source: The transmembrane topology and domain organization of LaINDY resemble that of VcINDY (Mancusso et al., 2012), with the scaffold domain being formed by transmembrane α-helices TMs 1–4 and 7–9, while the transport domain consists of TMs 5, 6, 10 and 11, as well as the helix hairpins HPin and HPout (Figure 3a-c).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3a-c and a citation to Mancusso et al., 2012.

claim: In LaINDY, a bend is found in the second helix of both hairpins, at Val163 in HPinb and Ala404 in HPoutb.
source: However, for both hairpins, a bend is found in the second helix, at Val163 in HPinb and Ala404 in HPoutb.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: LaINDY has an extrusion near the dimer interface into the periplasmic space formed by a sequence insertion between TM3 and TM4.
source: Another new structural feature of LaINDY is an extrusion near the dimer interface into the periplasmic space formed by a sequence insertion between TM3 and TM4.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: The scaffold and transport domains of LaINDY are linked via two horizontal helices and two loops near the membrane surface.
source: The scaffold and transport domains are linked via two horizontal helices and two loops near the membrane surface, H4c and L4-HPin on the cytosolic side and H9c and L9-HPout on the extracellular side (Figures 3c and 4a).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3c and 4a.

claim: A third linker between the scaffold and transport domains of LaINDY is formed by a cytoplasmic helix between TM6 and TM7 (H6b).
source: A third linker is formed by a cytoplasmic helix between TM6 and TM7 (H6b), where the equivalent region in VcINDY exists as a long loop (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The domain interface of LaINDY is largely formed by branched or short hydrophobic residues, with only two hydrogen bonds.
source: The domain interface is largely formed by branched or short hydrophobic residues, with only two hydrogen bonds.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The domain interface of LaINDY results in a smooth domain interface, similar to that observed in the elevator transporter GltPh.
source: This results in a smooth domain interface, similar to that observed in the elevator transporter GltPh (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and a citation to Reyes et al., 2009.

claim: While LaINDY's topology is similar to that of VcINDY, the relative domain positions are different.
source: While LaINDY's topology is similar to that of VcINDY, the relative domain positions are different.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: The transport domain of LaINDY is oriented toward the extracellular side with its substrate binding site facing the periplasm, yielding a Co conformation.
source: The transport domain is oriented toward the extracellular side with its substrate binding site facing the periplasm, yielding a Co conformation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The individual LaINDY and VcINDY domains exhibit strong structural homology, with backbone r.m.s.d.s of 2.897 Å and 2.044 Å for the scaffold and transport domains, respectively.
source: The individual LaINDY and VcINDY domains exhibit strong structural homology, with backbone r.m.s.d.s of 2.897 Å and 2.044 Å for the scaffold and transport domains, respectively (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the structures shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: Compared with VcINDY, the transport domain in LaINDY is repositioned by 13.0 Å towards the periplasm with a 37.4° rotation.
source: Compared with VcINDY, the transport domain in LaINDY is repositioned by 13.0 Å towards the periplasm with a 37.4° rotation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the structures shown in Figure 4.

claim: The domains' structural conservation and relative positions agree with the notion that DASS proteins operate via a rigid-body, elevator-type movement of the transport domain.
source: The domains' structural conservation and relative positions agree with the notion that DASS proteins operate via a rigid-body, elevator-type movement of the transport domain (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison, supported by Figure 1a.

claim: The structures of LaINDY determined in malate, αKG and in the malate/αKG mixture are in an outward-facing, substrate-bound (Co-S) state.
source: The structures of LaINDY determined in malate, αKG and in the malate/αKG mixture are in an outward-facing, substrate-bound (Co-S) state (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1j & k).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1j & k.

claim: The architecture of the LaINDY binding site is similar to that of VcINDY.
source: The architecture of the LaINDY binding site is similar to that of VcINDY.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Density corresponding to substrate is seen in the X-ray omit map of LaINDY-malate-αKG and in the LaINDY-αKG cryo-EM difference map.
source: Notably, within the binding site, density corresponding to substrate is seen in the X-ray omit map of LaINDY-malate-αKG, and in the LaINDY-αKG cryo-EM difference map, in a similar mode to substrate binding in VcINDY (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e & f).
evidence: This is supported by the electron density maps shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e & f.

claim: All three LaINDY Co-S structures are similar to each other and to the LaINDY Co apo structure, with pairwise r.m.s.d.s of 0.41–0.52 Å.
source: All three Co-S structures are not only similar to each other but, importantly, also to the LaINDY Co apo structure, with pairwise r.m.s.d.s of 0.41–0.52 Å (Figure 3f), indicating that substrate binding introduces little conformational change.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the structures shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Substrate binding to LaINDY introduces little conformational change.
source: All three Co-S structures are not only similar to each other but, importantly, also to the LaINDY Co apo structure, with pairwise r.m.s.d.s of 0.41–0.52 Å (Figure 3f), indicating that substrate binding introduces little conformational change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Major differences between LaINDY and VcINDY are seen at the cation binding sites.
source: In contrast to the similarity at the substrate binding site, major differences between LaINDY and VcINDY are seen at the cation binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a & c.

claim: At the Na1 site of VcINDY, an arginine (Arg159) is found in LaINDY, stabilized by a salt bridge with Glu146.
source: At the Na1 site of VcINDY (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f), an arginine (Arg159) is found in LaINDY, stabilized by a salt bridge with Glu146 (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a & c).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a & c.

claim: A histidine (His392) in LaINDY is located at the equivalent of the VcINDY Na2 site, with another histidine (His401) located 4 Å on its extracellular side.
source: Similarly, a histidine (His392) in LaINDY is located at the equivalent of the VcINDY Na2 site, with another histidine (His401) located 4 Å on its extracellular side.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Arg159 and His392 are conserved in DASS exchangers but absent in cotransporters.
source: Indeed, these residues are conserved in DASS exchangers but absent in cotransporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The cation binding sites are more completely enclosed by the surrounding loops in LaINDY compared to VcINDY.
source: Furthermore, the cation binding sites are more completely enclosed by the surrounding loops in LaINDY compared to VcINDY, facilitated by DASS exchanger specific insertions in the HPin and HPout and L10ab regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: It is unlikely that sodium ions bind to LaINDY as Na1 and Na2 do in VcINDY.
source: Based on these well enclosed and sterically occupied cation binding sites, it is unlikely that sodium ions bind to LaINDY as Na1 and Na2 do in VcINDY.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The authors hypothesize that the two positively-charged residues in exchangers act as permanent surrogates of the Na+ ions in cotransporters.
source: Rather, we hypothesize these two positively-charged residues in exchangers act as permanent surrogates of the Na+ ions in cotransporters.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on structural observations.

claim: Na+ ion substitutions have previously been observed in other transporters, which makes their substrate transport independent of sodium.
source: Such Na+ ion substitutions have previously been observed in other transporters, which makes their substrate transport independent of sodium (Shaffer et al., 2009; Kalayil et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shaffer et al., 2009; Kalayil et al., 2013.

claim: MD simulations of succinate-bound LaINDY revealed how the transition between its Co-S and Ci-S states is realized.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation systems of the Co-S and Co states of LaINDY were constructed from its X-ray crystal structure. Succinate was added to the X-ray crystal structure of LaINDY by aligning the cryo-EM structure of LaINDY with α-ketoglutarate bound and mutating the α-ketoglutarate into succinate.
evidence: This is a description of the computational approach.

claim: The transition between LaINDY's Co-S and Ci-S states consists of a 39° rigid-body rotation and an 8.3 Å translation of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain.
source: The transition consists of a 39° rigid-body rotation and an 8.3 Å translation of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–d and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–d and Video 2.

claim: The two 'arm' helices, H4c and H9c, are fixed in space with respect to the scaffold domain and cradle the transport domain during the Co-S to Ci-S transition.
source: The two 'arm' helices, H4c and H9c, are fixed in space with respect to the scaffold domain and cradle the transport domain during the Co-S to Ci-S transition (Figure 6c–e and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 6c–e and Video 3.

claim: Arm rigidity agrees with the conserved salt bridge between Arg122 and Glu283, and bulky-residue interactions at the elbows connecting H4c and H9c to the scaffold domain.
source: Such arm rigidity agrees with the conserved salt bridge, between Arg122 and Glu283, and bulky-residue interactions at the elbows connecting H4c and H9c to the scaffold domain (Figure 6a & b).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6a & b.

claim: The importance of the Arg122 to Glu283 salt bridge is consistent with recent observations in NaCT, where transport activity was abolished by mutations of the equivalent arginine.
source: The importance of the Arg122 to Glu283 salt bridge is also consistent with recent observations in NaCT, where transport activity was abolished by mutations of the equivalent arginine (Khamaysi et al., 2020), probably by disrupting the conserved salt bridge between H4c and TM7.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Khamaysi et al., 2020.

claim: Flexibility of the hinge loops L4-HPin and L9-HPout at the other end of the arm helices allows transport domain movement.
source: In contrast to the rigidity at the elbows, flexibility of the hinge loops L4-HPin and L9-HPout at the other end of the arm helices allows transport domain movement (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: During the Co-S to Ci-S transition the angle between the arm helices and the hairpin helices changes by approximately 30° at both hinges.
source: During the Co-S to Ci-S transition the angle between the arm helices and the hairpin helices changes by approximately 30° at both hinges (Figure 6f), allowing the overall rotation and translation of the transport domain.
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Despite the large domain movements of LaINDY during MD simulations of the Co-S to Ci-S transition, succinate stably binds without significant changes within the binding site.
source: Despite the large domain movements of LaINDY during MD simulations of the Co-S to Ci-S transition, succinate stably binds without significant changes within the binding site (Figure 5b), though the depth of substrate binding correlates with the orientation of Asn156 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1g,h & l).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1g,h & l.

claim: The conformations and interactions of the Na+ surrogate side chains, Arg159 and His392, are generally stable through the conformational transition.
source: Furthermore, the conformations and interactions of the Na+ surrogate side chains, Arg159 and His392, are generally stable through the conformational transition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b & d).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b & d.

claim: The two cryo-EM structures of VcINDY are in a substrate-free, inward-facing (Ci-Na+) state.
source: The two cryo-EM structures of VcINDY are in a substrate-free, inward-facing (Ci-Na+) state (Figure 1b & c) and provide an opportunity to describe the conformational changes that occur upon substrate release.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1b & c.

claim: The Ci-Na+ VcINDY structures are very similar to each other, with an r.m.s.d of 0.75 Å.
source: The Ci-Na+ VcINDY structures are very similar to each other, with an r.m.s.d of 0.75 Å (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the structures shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Compared with the Ci-Na+-S structures, the substrate-free VcINDY structures display local changes throughout the protein.
source: However, compared with the Ci-Na+-S structures, the substrate-free structures display local changes throughout the protein.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7.

claim: At the substrate binding site of both cryo-EM VcINDY structures, Pro422 at the N-terminus of TM10b in the substrate free structures moved by up to 1.5 Å.
source: At the substrate binding site of both cryo-EM VcINDY structures, Pro422 at the N-terminus of TM10b in the substrate free structures moved by up to 1.5 Å (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Concurrently with Pro422 movement, on the cytoplasmic surface, His432 at the C-terminus of TM10b is rotated by 73°.
source: Concurrently, on the cytoplasmic surface, His432 at the C-terminus of the same helix is rotated by 73° (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The movement of His432 causes a steric clash with its neighbor, Tyr178 of TM5a, inducing a rotation in that side chain by 41°.
source: This movement of His432 causes a steric clash with its neighbor, Tyr178 of TM5a, inducing a rotation in that side chain by 41°.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7a.

claim: One helix turn away from Tyr178, the side chain of Arg175 moves closer to Glu437 of TM11, forming a salt bridge.
source: One helix turn away, the side chain of Arg175 moves closer to Glu437 of TM11, forming a salt bridge.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7a.

claim: These rearrangements lead to movements of HPina, HPinb and TM5a by 1.4 Å toward the scaffold domain.
source: These rearrangements lead to movements of HPina, HPinb and TM5a by 1.4 Å toward the scaffold domain.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Human NaCT's transport activity is abolished when the equivalent of Glu437 is mutated to histidine, resulting in SLC13A5 Deficiency.
source: Supporting the importance of these interactions, human NaCT's transport activity is abolished when the equivalent of Glu437 is mutated to histidine, resulting in SLC13A5 Deficiency (Hardies et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hardies et al., 2015.

claim: Comparison of the Ci-Na+-S and Ci-Na+ VcINDY structures revealed prominent changes on the periplasmic surface.
source: Comparison of the previous Ci-Na+-S (Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017) and amphipol preserved Ci-Na+ VcINDY structures also revealed prominent changes on the periplasmic surface (Figure 7b and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7b and Video 4.

claim: The loop connecting HPoutb and TM10a, from Ala395 to Pro400, has moved on the periplasmic surface in the Ci-Na+ structure.
source: The loop connecting HPoutb and TM10a, from Ala395 to Pro400, has moved on the periplasmic surface.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The C-terminus of HPoutb unwinds by one turn (Val392 – Glu394) in the amphipol structure.
source: The C-terminus of HPoutb also unwinds by one turn (Val392 – Glu394) in the amphipol structure.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: As a result of HPoutb unwinding, the conserved salt bridge between Glu394 with Lys337 of H9b from the scaffold domain breaks, and Phe396 moves away from its contact with H9c.
source: As a result, the conserved salt bridge between Glu394 with Lys337 of H9b from the scaffold domain breaks, and Phe396 moves away from its contact with H9c.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Structural changes in VcINDY agree with observations of human NaCT mutations at positions equivalent to Pro400 and Val401, which abolish transport and cause SLC13A5 Deficiency.
source: Such structural changes agree with observations of human NaCT mutations, at positions equivalent to Pro400 and Val401 in VcINDY, which abolish transport and cause SLC13A5 Deficiency (Thevenon et al., 2014; Klotz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thevenon et al., 2014; Klotz et al., 2016.

claim: The side chain of Trp461 is inserted between TM6, TM10a and TM11, packing against another conserved aromatic residue, Phe220.
source: Finally, the side chain of Trp461 is inserted between TM6, TM10a and TM11, packing against another conserved aromatic residue, Phe220.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: When bound to Fab84, the loop connecting HPoutb and TM10a in VcINDY is midway between the Ci-Na+-S and Ci-Na+ structures.
source: Notably, when bound to Fab84, the loop connecting HPoutb and TM10a in VcINDY is midway between the Ci-Na+-S and Ci-Na+ structures.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c & d.

claim: Fab84's epitope covers the periplasmic surface of VcINDY and binds both apo and substrate-bound states.
source: This agrees with Fab84's epitope covering the periplasmic surface of VcINDY and binding both apo and substrate-bound states (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c & d).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c & d.

claim: A complete lipid molecule from the periplasmic leaflet was found at the interface between the transport and scaffold domains of VcINDY.
source: Also, a complete lipid molecule from the periplasmic leaflet was found at the interface between the transport and scaffold domains, interacting with TM1, TM2 and HPouta, and therefore may be involved in regulating conformational changes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The lipid molecule at the domain interface may be involved in regulating conformational changes.
source: Also, a complete lipid molecule from the periplasmic leaflet was found at the interface between the transport and scaffold domains, interacting with TM1, TM2 and HPouta, and therefore may be involved in regulating conformational changes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The authors report cryo-EM and X-ray structures of two DASS proteins in four states.
source: In this work, we report cryo-EM and X-ray structures of two DASS proteins in four states as well as MD simulations of the Co-S to Ci-S transition.
evidence: This is a summary of the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ci-Na+, Co, and Co-S are previously un-observed states of the DASS transport cycle.
source: Of these structures, the Ci-Na+, Co, and Co-S are previously un-observed states of the DASS transport cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the results.

claim: Together with the previously published structures of VcINDY in its Ci-Na+-S state, these results give a much clearer understanding of the structural basis of transport.
source: Together with the previously published structures of VcINDY in its Ci-Na+-S state, these results give us a much clearer understanding of the structural basis of transport.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the results.

claim: The gallery of structures allows the authors to more completely characterize the reaction cycle of DASS transporters.
source: The gallery of structures allows us to more completely characterize the reaction cycle of DASS transporters.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the results.

claim: The authors advance the elevator mechanism of the DASS family from a conceptual model into an atomic description of the transport domain's movement within the framework of the scaffold domain.
source: Thereby, we advance the elevator mechanism of the family from a conceptual model into an atomic description of the transport domain's movement within the framework of the scaffold domain.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the results.

claim: The structures of LaINDY represent the first outward-facing structures of any DASS family protein.
source: The structures of LaINDY that we have determined represent the first outward-facing structures of any DASS family protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the results.

claim: The LaINDY structures generally agree with a previous model of VcINDY in its Co conformation, with an r.m.s.d of 3.7 Å for the backbone atoms.
source: These structures generally agree with a previous model of VcINDY in its Co conformation (Mulligan et al., 2016), proposed based on the inverted-topology structural repeat and cross-linking distance constraints, with an r.m.s.d of 3.7 Å for the backbone atoms.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with a previous model, supported by a citation to Mulligan et al., 2016.

claim: The occupation of the Na1 and Na2 sites by conserved basic residues, and absence of any other apparent sodium densities, suggest LaINDY is a DASS exchanger.
source: As noted, the occupation of the Na1 and Na2 sites by conserved basic residues, and absence of any other apparent sodium densities, suggest LaINDY is a DASS exchanger.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: LaINDY's classification as a DASS exchanger is supported by its phylogeny and ability to catalyze succinate-dicarboxylate exchange.
source: This is supported by its phylogeny and ability to catalyze succinate-dicarboxylate exchange.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and the transport assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Further experiments, preferably in reconstituted proteoliposomes, will be needed to examine the sodium and proton dependence of LaINDY transport, and confirm strict substrate coupling in the exchange reaction.
source: However, further experiments, preferably in reconstituted proteoliposomes, will be needed to examine the sodium and proton dependence of transport, and confirm strict substrate coupling in the exchange reaction.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed to confirm the findings.

claim: Comparison of the outward-facing and the inward-facing structures, along with MD simulation results, suggests how a DASS protein operates through an elevator-type movement of the transport domain within each protomer.
source: Comparison of the outward-facing and the inward-facing structures, along with MD simulation results, immediately suggests how a DASS protein operates through an elevator-type movement of the transport domain within each protomer (Figure 6c & d).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and MD simulations, supported by Figure 6c & d.

claim: The transport domain moves within the framework formed by the two horizontal α-helix arms on opposing membrane surfaces during the reaction cycle, alternating the substrate binding site between the two sides of the membrane.
source: The transport domain moves within the framework formed by the two horizontal α-helix arms on opposing membrane surfaces during the reaction cycle, alternating the substrate binding site between the two sides of the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and MD simulations.

claim: The DASS mechanism is similar to that proposed for the glutamate transporter GltPh, although the two arms of GltPh are not on the membrane surface but rather transmembrane helices.
source: This mechanism is similar to that proposed for the glutamate transporter GltPh, although the two arms of GltPh are not on the membrane surface but rather transmembrane helices (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison with another transporter, supported by a citation to Reyes et al., 2009.

claim: Analyzing the various conformations enables the authors to suggest how substrate binding leads to transporter conformational changes while preventing slippage.
source: Analyzing the various conformations also enables us to suggest how substrate binding leads to transporter conformational changes while preventing slippage, or unproductive Co to Ci transitions.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the results.

claim: DASS cotransporters and exchangers appear to employ both unique and shared mechanisms to prevent slippage.
source: In this regard, DASS cotransporters and exchangers appear to employ both unique and shared mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Previous experimental data support that Na+-driven DASS cotransporters operate via an ordered sequence, namely, Na+ binding induces substrate binding, while substrate release precedes Na+ release.
source: Previous experimental data support that Na+-driven DASS cotransporters operate via an ordered sequence (Wright et al., 1983; Yao and Pajor, 2000; Hall and Pajor, 2005; Pajor et al., 2013; Mulligan et al., 2014), namely, Na+ binding induces substrate binding, while substrate release precedes Na+ release.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wright et al., 1983; Yao and Pajor, 2000; Hall and Pajor, 2005; Pajor et al., 2013; Mulligan et al., 2014.

claim: For VcINDY, substrate release in the cytoplasm induces conformational changes as the transporter transitions between the Ci-Na+-S and Ci-Na+ states.
source: For VcINDY, we have now observed that substrate release in the cytoplasm induces conformational changes as the transporter transitions between the Ci-Na+-S and Ci-Na+ states.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7.

claim: Substrate release in VcINDY leads to an unwinding of the C-terminus of TM11, loop movements, and side chain rotations, resulting in significant changes in local helix packing and protein compactness.
source: Specifically, substrate release leads to an unwinding of the C-terminus of TM11, loop movements, and side chain rotations, resulting in significant changes in local helix packing and protein compactness (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mechanism of VcINDY is distinguished from GltPh and homologs in which one or two hairpin gates directly pack against the scaffold domain and block unproductive conformational changes.
source: This is distinguished from GltPh and homologs in which one or two hairpin gates directly pack against the scaffold domain and block unproductive conformational changes (Reyes et al., 2009; Garaeva et al., 2019; Arkhipova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with other transporters, supported by citations to Reyes et al., 2009; Garaeva et al., 2019; Arkhipova et al., 2020.

claim: The exchanger LaINDY exhibits no major conformational changes between the apo and substrate-bound outward-facing states.
source: In contrast, the exchanger LaINDY exhibits no major conformational changes between the apo and substrate-bound outward-facing states.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The authors propose that DASS exchangers limit slippage via a charge compensation mechanism.
source: As two positively-charged residues are found to occupy the cation binding sites, we propose that the DASS exchangers limit slippage, or unproductive conformational changes, via a charge compensation mechanism.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: In the apo state of DASS exchangers, where the binding sites have a net positive charge, the hydrophobic surface of the scaffold domain would be an electrostatic barrier to the movement of the transport domain.
source: In the apo state, where the binding sites have a net positive charge, the hydrophobic surface of the scaffold domain would be an electrostatic barrier to the movement of the transport domain.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: Only when divalent substrate binds and the net charge is neutralized can the DASS exchanger freely exchange between the Ci and Co conformations, ensuring a one-to-one stoichiometric exchange of substrates.
source: Only when divalent substrate binds and the net charge is neutralized can the transporter freely exchange between the Ci and Co conformations, ensuring a one-to-one stoichiometric exchange of substrates.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: In addition to substrate-release induced conformational changes, charge compensation is also essential to avoid slippage, ensuring Na+-substrate coupling in DASS cotransporters.
source: In addition to the noted substrate-release induced conformational changes, charge compensation is also essential to avoid slippage, ensuring Na+-substrate coupling in DASS cotransporters.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: The Na+ ions at the Na1 and Na2 sites in cotransporters can be regarded as equivalent to the cationic side chains of exchangers, though Na+ reversibly binds.
source: In fact, the Na+ ions at the Na1 and Na2 sites in cotransporters can be regarded as equivalent to the cationic side chains of exchangers, though Na+ reversibly binds.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: In cotransporters, the charge compensation model predicts that the transporter can only transition between Co and Ci conformations when the transport domain is either fully-loaded or fully-unloaded.
source: In cotransporters, the charge compensation model predicts that the transporter can only transition between Co and Ci conformations when the transport domain is either fully-loaded or fully-unloaded.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed charge compensation mechanism.

claim: The charge compensation mechanism ensures tightly coupled import of Na+ and substrate in cotransporters, while the reversible binding of Na+ allows for the concentration of the divalent substrate against its electrochemical gradient.
source: Such a mechanism ensures tightly coupled import of Na+ and substrate in cotransporters, while the reversible binding of Na+ allows for the concentration of the divalent substrate against its electrochemical gradient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed charge compensation mechanism.

claim: Similar charge compensation mechanisms have been proposed for the citrate transporter CitS and the glutamate transporter EAAC1.
source: Similar charge compensation mechanisms have been proposed for the citrate transporter CitS and the glutamate transporter EAAC1 (Lolkema and Slotboom, 2017; Grewer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lolkema and Slotboom, 2017; Grewer et al., 2012.
